extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians and readers following the Mochizuki–Scholze/Stix debate (number theorists, arithmetic geometers, mathematical community)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and norms for assessing the correctness, clarity, and publishability of a claimed mathematical proof, and for how authors, referees, and editors should behave in such disputes. Focused on the Mochizuki IUT / abc-proof controversy but generalizable to high-level mathematical proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof must convince other experts / communicability
rubrics_metrics.description: “Is not the whole point of a proof that it is an argument that convinces someone else?! If you can’t prove a thing to at least one other person, have you not by definition failed to prove anything? Failure to be understood is the fault of the speaker!”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claimed proof must be presented so that other competent experts can follow and be convinced by the argument. If no experts can be persuaded, the claim has failed. Anti-pattern: treating unverifiability as the author's prerogative or blaming readers for not spending indefinite time to understand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden on prover to convince experts / respond to objections
rubrics_metrics.description: “The burden is on the mathematician who believes they have a proof to convince other experts... One can argue about the wide variety of claims he makes in response ... but the bottom line is that they found them unconvincing.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors who claim a proof must address specific technical objections raised by experts with clear, focused, technical rebuttals. Merely asserting that critics are incompetent or demanding prolonged private study is not an acceptable substitute. Example: identify the exact logical step the critics say is flawed and provide a concise correction or demonstration why the criticism is mistaken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referees are not obligated to continue indefinitely after finding an error
rubrics_metrics.description: “It’s not the responsibility of the referees to keep working on this, once they feel they have found an error, explained what it is, and the author has no convincing response.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If referees identify a substantive gap or error and the author fails to provide a convincing fix, referees may stop further detailed engagement; they are under no duty to carry the author's burden of repair. Anti-pattern: expecting referees to do the work of rewriting or filling the gap for the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplifications used in critiques must be proven/justified
rubrics_metrics.description: “‘drastic simplifications’ should be proven, otherwise they are just conjectures. Claiming that ‘Mochizuki was not able to convince us’ doesn’t prove these conjectures.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a critic analyzes a allegedly simpler model of an argument, they must prove that the simplification preserves the essential structure relevant to the disputed conclusion. Otherwise the simplification may create a spurious counterexample (a straw man). Anti-pattern: relying on unproven simplifications and treating negative conclusions about the simplified model as automatically transferring to the original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and technical precision preferred to lengthy analogy or rhetoric
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments note that Mochizuki’s lengthy analogies and extended exposition are ‘not technically precise enough’ and that a short concrete rebuttal would be preferable: “Mochizuki could make a very short and concrete rebuttal ... but no, it needs a 41-page report…”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responses to specific objections should be concise, technical, and targeted at the disputed point. Long, sweeping analogies or rhetorical flourishes that do not pinpoint the alleged mistake are unlikely to convince experts. Example: provide a direct argument showing why the critic’s step fails, rather than extensive philosophical remarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ad hominem attacks; keep focus on mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple commenters: the personal attacks and sensationalistic remarks ‘weaken the argument’ and ‘are not helpful’—‘People should just focus on the math.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal insults, questioning competence, or rhetorical theatrics undermine the author’s credibility and distract from mathematical issues. Maintain professional tone; focus rebuttals on the mathematical content. Anti-pattern: lengthy public denunciations of critics’ intelligence or motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial responsibility: journals should not publish mutually incompatible papers
rubrics_metrics.description: “I don’t think any journal would even consider publishing both of these, the editor would just say ‘one or both of them is wrong, if we publish both, we’d be publishing an incorrect paper’.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should assess referee reports and the author’s responses and avoid accepting a paper that, in light of expert objections, appears to contain an unaddressed substantive gap. If a dispute remains, editors may require resolution before publication. Anti-pattern: publishing a contested proof without adequate expert clearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification claims (seminars, repeated reading) are not substitutes for addressing concrete objections
rubrics_metrics.description: Fesenko claims IUT has been ‘verified at least 30 times’ in seminars, but commenters observe that repeated exposure is not persuasive if specific objections are not directly answered: ‘This collection of mathematicians has ... been actively involved in detailed discussions ...’ yet others find the specific Scholze–Stix objection unaddressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims of wide informal verification (seminars, repeated readings) do not relieve the author of responding to pointed technical critiques. Concrete, public rebuttals to explicit objections are required. Anti-pattern: asserting broad community understanding as evidence without showing how objections are resolved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors should revise exposition when experts indicate gaps
rubrics_metrics.description: “Normally if an expert tells you he thinks there’s a gap or mistake in your manuscript giving a proof ... you take this as an indication that you did not explain things well enough. Mochizuki is not just taking the attitude that there’s nothing wrong ... he’s also taking the attitude that he does not need to even try to improve its exposition.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When specialists point to unclear or missing steps, authors are expected to improve exposition, clarify definitions, and supply missing rationale. Failure to do so reduces the chances of convincing referees and readers. Example: include additional lemmas, clearer definitions, or worked examples that illuminate difficult steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be specific: identify exact error or demonstrate convincingly why critics are wrong
rubrics_metrics.description: “Someone will have to identify a serious flaw in their argument, in a convincing way.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either pinpoint the precise logical error in the critics’ reasoning or supply a clear counter-argument showing they misapplied or misunderstood your construction. Vague assertions that critics are ignorant are insufficient. Scoring note: clarity and specificity of the corrective argument determine persuasiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid creating a straw-man by oversimplifying the original argument
rubrics_metrics.description: “What Mochizuki claims and what Scholze and Stix themselves admit being possible, is that Scholze and Stix with their simplifications have constructed the mathematical equivalent of a Straw man argument.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reducing an argument to a simpler form for analysis, ensure the reduction preserves the properties used in the original derivation. If the simplification removes essential structure, the critique may attack a non-equivalent target. Anti-pattern: concluding the original is invalid solely because a simplified version fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community consensus should emerge from expert convergence
rubrics_metrics.description: “Experts discussing a technical question about a proof are supposed to converge on an understanding of what is correct and what isn’t.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The norm in mathematics is that public, technical exchange among experts will lead to consensus about correctness. Persistent irreconcilable camps are unusual; resolution typically comes from concrete fixes or clearer exposition that persuades a critical mass of experts. Monitoring convergence of reputable specialists is a practical criterion for assessing the status of a disputed proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional presentation and credibility matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments note that odd site content and legal proscriptions on an author’s web page ‘does not give a professional impression’ and may undermine credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-mathematical aspects (professional, clear web pages; avoidance of bizarre legal notices or irrelevant graphics) influence how the mathematical community perceives an author’s seriousness. While not determinative of correctness, sloppy or eccentric presentation can reduce willingness to engage constructively. Anti-pattern: allowing distracting or puzzling website content to overshadow technical submissions.
